stimulus.text: An engraving published in 1874 imagining John Rolfe at work in Virginia. A single man in 17th-century dress hoes young tobacco plants by hand among rows of small plants.
stimulus.source_note: Engraving published 1874, imagining John Rolfe; public domain (pre-1930). The image is a 19th-century imagining, not a 17th-century record.

source: original; stimulus is a real historical image from the shared pool

books.section: Topic 2.6 Slavery in the British Colonies

stem: What limits the use of this engraving as evidence about tobacco farming in Virginia in the 1610s?

options.text: The engraving shows only one man, so it proves tobacco farming used no enslaved labor.
options.misconception: One figure cannot prove who did the work; the image shows a single imagined scene.

options.text: The engraving is a drawing, so it cannot show anything true about the past.
options.misconception: Drawings can show true things, but this one is a later imagining — the limit is its date, not its medium.

options.text: It was made in 1874, so it shows how 19th-century Americans pictured Rolfe, not 1610s farming.
The engraving shows tobacco plants, so it proves Rolfe invented tobacco farming.
options.misconception: Native peoples grew tobacco long before Rolfe; he made it a cash crop.

rationales.general:
1. Read the date on the image. It was published in 1874 — more than two centuries after the 1610s.
2. Ask what an 1874 artist could know about 1610s farming. Only what books and stories told him; he was imagining, not recording.
3. Ask what the image can still show. How 19th-century Americans pictured Rolfe and the tobacco frontier.
4. Name the limit. It is evidence about 1874, not about 1610.
Remember: always check an image's date before you trust it as evidence — a late picture tells you about its own time.
rationales.C: The engraving was published in 1874, more than two centuries after the 1610s it pictures. An artist working in 1874 could only imagine Rolfe's Virginia from books and stories — he was not recording what he saw. So the image is evidence about 19th-century Americans and how they pictured the tobacco frontier, not evidence about 1610s farming. The other options are wrong: a single figure proves nothing about the workforce, and drawings can show true things. Background: Native peoples grew tobacco long before Rolfe.
rationales.A: One figure cannot prove who did the work; the image shows a single imagined scene.
rationales.B: Drawings can show true things, but this one is a later imagining — the limit is its date, not its medium.
rationales.D: Background: Native peoples grew tobacco long before Rolfe; he made it a cash crop.
